Chapter 6: When the Old Stories No Longer Fit
You know, sometimes the stories we tell ourselves about who we are and how the world works become so familiar, we barely even notice them anymore.
But think about it—these old stories shape our choices, our relationships, and even what we believe is possible for us.
So, what happens when those stories just... stop working? When the scripts we’ve repeated for years—like “I have to be perfect,” or “I’m unlovable,” or “I always have to be the strong one”—start to feel less like comfort, and more like cages?
In the quiet space of the therapy room, things start to unravel. The therapist—now in the role of a patient herself—realizes she’s been clinging to beliefs that once helped her survive, but now only keep her feeling stuck.
She catches herself replaying the same old patterns: blaming herself for the breakup, doubting her own worth, worrying she’ll never find love again.
Each session turns into a gentle invitation to look at these beliefs, to ask where they really came from, and to wonder... are they even true anymore?
One afternoon, a client sits across from her, wrestling with something so familiar. He’s always seen himself as the “fixer” in his family—the one who holds everything together.
But now, he’s just tired. He’s exhausted, even resentful. And for the first time, he wonders if it might be okay to let go of that role.
The idea is terrifying. Who would he be, if he wasn’t the fixer? What if people stopped needing him?
The therapist sees the fear in his eyes. She’s felt it, too—that anxiety that comes with letting go of an identity, even one that hurts.
Together, they start to explore what it could look like to write a new story. One that allows for rest, for imperfection, even for asking others for help.
There’s another client—a woman who’s spent years believing she’s “too much” for anyone to love. In therapy, she traces that story all the way back to childhood, to moments when her big feelings were met with criticism, or maybe just silence.
Slowly, she starts to imagine a different possibility: maybe her emotions aren’t a flaw at all. Maybe they’re actually a strength.
What really stands out is this—changing our stories isn’t about erasing the past.
It’s about seeing it in a new way, with compassion instead of judgment.
The therapist begins to loosen her grip on those old scripts, too. She realizes that healing means letting herself be more than just the sum of her wounds.
